subject: snail kite
title: A Snail 5 Times Bigger Arrived, and This Bird's Beak Grew to Match

scenes.text: An invasive snail should have finished this bird off. It didn't.
Florida's snail kite eats almost nothing but apple snails, plucked from the marsh.
By the late two-thousands, only about seven hundred were left.
Then a South American apple snail invaded, up to five times bigger than the native one.
Small-beaked kites struggled with the giants. Young birds with bigger beaks survived their first year far better.
Within about ten years, the kites' beaks had measurably grown. Their food got bigger, so they did.

description:
Florida's endangered snail kite fell from about 3,500 birds to about 700 in the 2000s.
Then the island apple snail, two to five times bigger than the native snail, invaded. Kites with larger beaks handled the giant snails better, and young birds with bigger beaks survived their first year far better.
In about ten years, less than two generations, average beak size grew measurably (Nature Ecology and Evolution, 2017).
Can you think of another animal evolving this fast?
first_comment: Each kite eats thousands of snails a year, one at a time, pried out with that hooked beak. Is this evolution or just the lucky big-beaked birds surviving?
